title: Historical Nuremberg Great Clock
intro: The Nuremberg Great Clock represents the historical civic convention of counting separate equal day and night hours, with their allocation changing on prescribed turning days (Wendetage).
structure: Daylight allocation varies from 8 to 16 hours over the annual schedule, with the complementary number assigned to night. The day interval is centred on apparent solar noon at Nuremberg. NUR-D counts from the scheduled day start; NUR-N counts from the scheduled night start. Both begin at zero.
example: With a 16-hour day allocation, day begins at 04:00 apparent solar time and ends at 20:00. At apparent solar noon the display is 08:00 NUR-D; at apparent midnight it is 04:00 NUR-N.
history: The fixed schedule projects the documented 1488 Julian turning days onto their proleptic Gregorian seasonal equivalents (nine days later at that epoch). It is not a daily measured sunrise/sunset schedule.
model: Use Gregorian day of year; leap years shift thresholds from day 71 onward by one day. The provider uses fixed Nuremberg longitude 11.0767 degrees east and compact apparent solar time. For N allocated day hours, start = (24-N)/2 and end = start+N. Count elapsed equal hours from the selected boundary, wrap night across midnight, and schedule the next rendered change.
limits: The user's coordinates and civil offset do not affect this fixed historical-city profile. Its annual repetition and modern solar approximation do not establish exact historic clock readings. The Nuremberg-style local solar provider is a separate model.
